title: Running a personal credential audit
body_md:
## Audit the routes that still work

A credential audit is a review of *current access*, not a ritual of changing every password each year. Start with accounts that unlock others or can cause material harm: primary email, password manager, financial services and work identity. The right order follows impact and evidence. A reported compromise or reused password needs prompt action; a unique password with no concern does not need scheduled rotation merely because a calendar changed.

### Build a small, usable inventory

For each priority account, record the service name, independently verified sign-in address, whether its password is unique, which MFA methods are accepted, where recovery goes, and which devices or sessions remain signed in. Do not write actual passwords or recovery codes in the inventory; the manager and protected backup hold those. Your manager's health view may flag reused or known-compromised entries, but assess findings against the actual service. HIBP can identify indexed incidents associated with an email address; it does not reveal which password belonged to that address, and no result is not an all-clear.

Next inspect live access. Remove unfamiliar sessions or stale trusted devices through the real account settings, but verify a device name before declaring an intrusion: one physical device can produce several sessions, and names can change. Check app passwords, connected apps and API tokens where the service offers them. Revoke a grant only after identifying what uses it; a legitimate mail client or automation may stop working. If an unfamiliar session is credible, secure the device, change relevant credentials, inspect recovery and forwarding rules, and report through the provider or workplace channel. A password change may not revoke every token or session automatically.

### Make it maintainable

Review the top accounts now, then extend to lower-priority ones. Repeat after a breach, device loss, job change or recovery-contact change, and set a personal reminder for periodic review rather than promising a universal “one-hour annual fix.” Make a separate emergency-access plan for the vault according to its actual features and your wishes. Emergency access is a deliberate trust choice; it is not a default checkbox or a reason to hand someone your primary passphrase.

Finish with a short result: which reuse was removed, which MFA or recovery route improved, which suspicious activity requires follow-up, and which service limits stronger controls. This makes the next audit easier and keeps uncertainty visible.

widget_config.goal: Prioritise an account-access audit and distinguish urgent compromise from normal, legitimate account activity.
widget_config.today_action: Make a five-account inventory without secrets: unique password status, MFA, recovery, sessions and connected apps; resolve one high-impact finding through the service’s own settings.
widget_config.scope: General educational audit method; service controls, workplace policy and incident response vary. HIBP coverage is incomplete. Checked 2026-10-20.

sources.title: Have I Been Pwned: Frequently Asked Questions
sources.scope: Service documentation; a listed address is not proof that its password leaked; coverage is incomplete.

blocks.title: Unexpected token in a developer account
blocks.situation: A synthetic personal code-hosting account lists an API token with a name you do not recognise and broad access. Its sign-in password is unique.
blocks.analysis: A unique password does not neutralise a token already granted. Identify the token’s use, revoke it if unowned, inspect activity, rotate affected secrets as appropriate and report to the provider or employer if it is a work account.

blocks.title: Two sessions from one familiar laptop
blocks.situation: A synthetic email service lists two sessions with slightly different browser labels at your home location. Both timestamps match your recent use.
blocks.analysis: Multiple rows are not proof of compromise. Confirm details through the service’s own device view; sign out any session you cannot explain, but avoid calling the legitimate duplicate an attack without evidence.

blocks.title: Triage five priority accounts
blocks.setup: Synthetic audit sheet: email has a reused password; a shop has a breach notice; a code-hosting account shows an unknown token; a travel app has two familiar sessions; the vault has MFA.

choices.text: Replace the reused primary-email password with a unique one and review its MFA.
choices.explanation: The email account may reset several others.

choices.text: Rename the two familiar travel-app sessions.
choices.explanation: Session labels are lower priority than a reused email secret.

steps.prompt: The shop appears in HIBP, but its provider says only names were exposed. What do you record?

choices.text: Record the known data category and check the provider notice; do not infer password theft from the email hit.
choices.consequence: The audit preserves what is known and unknown.
choices.explanation: HIBP address search does not identify a leaked password for that account.

choices.text: Record that the shop password definitely leaked.
choices.consequence: A false conclusion enters the audit.
choices.explanation: The indexed address alone is not enough evidence.

steps.prompt: The unknown code-hosting token has broad access. What next?

choices.text: Identify ownership and recent use, then revoke if unowned and inspect activity.
choices.consequence: A potentially live alternate access route is handled.
choices.explanation: Tokens can work independently of the login password; avoid breaking a known integration blindly.

choices.text: Change the password only and assume all tokens disappear.
choices.explanation: Token revocation is a separate control on many services.

steps.prompt: Two travel-app sessions match your laptop use. How should you close the review?

choices.text: Verify session details, note the explanation, and sign out only anything still unexplained.
choices.consequence: Legitimate activity is not mislabeled as an incident.
choices.explanation: An audit distinguishes evidence from suspicion.

choices.text: Report a confirmed intrusion based only on two labels.
choices.explanation: One device can have multiple sessions.

blocks.debrief: A useful audit prioritises impact, traces evidence and checks alternate access. Retry a decision that confused an indicator with proof.

questions.prompt: A unique password has no breach indication. What is the reason to change it today?

choices.text: There may be none; prioritise evidence of compromise, reuse or weakness.
choices.explanation: Calendar-only rotation is not the core audit action.

choices.text: Every password must be changed annually regardless of evidence.
choices.explanation: Routine rotation can add work without addressing active access.

questions.prompt: A connected app still has access after you change the account password. Why?

choices.text: App grants or tokens can be independent and may need separate revocation.
A password change always revokes every connected app.
choices.explanation: Service behaviour varies; do not assume it.

questions.prompt: A breach database has no entry for an address. What can the audit say?

choices.text: No indexed result was found there; it cannot certify no exposure.
choices.explanation: Coverage is limited to data the service has indexed.

choices.text: The address and all its accounts are confirmed safe.
choices.explanation: No single database provides that proof.
